title: The robe and the door
hookLine: deeds shape the body we are given; grace opens the door
carry: deeds shape the robe; grace opens the door

cards: Two words side by side in the fourth pauri of Japji: karmi, nadri. In paraphrase, the line runs: by deeds comes the robe; by grace, the door of liberation. A robe and a door.

An odd pair for one breath. A robe is something you're wrapped in every day; it takes the shape of you. A door is something you can stand in front of for a very long time and never open with your own hand.
Today's word is the first half: karam.

teach.b: The robe first. Sikh readers take the robe in this line as the body, the life we're given. Karam is deeds, actions and their weight.
What we have done shapes what we carry: the body, the circumstances, the habits that wrap around us. On its own, that would be a strict ledger. Then the door.
Nadar is the glance, the gracious look of the One.
The line says the door of liberation opens by nadar, not by karam.

teach.h: NOT A LEDGER, NOT AN EXCUSE.
teach.b: You can do good for a lifetime, and the door still isn't something you buy. It is given. Why both?
If the line said only deeds, life would be bookkeeping, and anyone behind would stay behind. If it said only grace, there'd be no reason to do good at all.
Guru Nanak keeps both: deeds really do shape us, and the last step is a gift. The same pauri closes, in paraphrase: the True One is all of it. Readers hold the line in two ways.
Some Sikh interpreters read karmi itself as grace, so the robe, too, would be a gift. Others read it as deeds, as today does. Both readings keep grace at the door.

teach.h: DO THE GOOD; LEAVE THE DOOR.
teach.b: So the life this points to looks like yesterday's farmer: do the good in front of you with your whole heart, and leave the door to the giver.

how: Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning, including the line about deeds and the robe, grace and the door, and Sikh life joins seva and honest work with remembrance and trust in the Guru's grace.

o: deeds, actions and the weight they carry
a fixed destiny you can never change
a reward handed out for praying often

games.q: the robe and the door: tap the pairs.

s: in Japji, good deeds alone open the door of liberation
deeds shape the robe; the door opens by nadar, grace.
some Sikh interpreters read karmi in this line as grace too
others read it as deeds; both keep grace at the door.
the line pairs a robe and a door

games.q: you've done good deeds all your life, and you're standing at the door of liberation. what opens it?
o: the total of your deeds, added up.
nadar, the gracious glance of the One.
games.why: Japji: by deeds comes the robe; by grace, the door. deeds matter, and the last step is a gift.

practice: Picture one good deed within reach today, carrying something for someone, a kind word to a coworker, a bill paid fairly, and see yourself doing it.

Let the picture end the moment the deed is done, and let the result belong to someone else. If you pray, let that letting go become a hope for grace; if you don't, just feel the difference between doing and receiving.

wordCard.voice: Karam. Deeds, actions and their weight: in Japji, by deeds comes the robe, and by grace, nadar, the door of liberation. Today's word.
